players.product: grid-scale battery energy storage (BESS) for data-center/grid power

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 execution and FY2027 capacity setup. CFO Ahmed Pasha: the EBITDA guidance range is wider than the revenue range only to cover additional costs Fluence may incur as it ramps operations ('we have still some work to do on execution'), and asked whether Q4 revenue carries much EPC work: 'No, I don't think' — 'Most of that is in the U.S., and that's mostly the deliveries that we have under our domestic content.' CEO Julian Nebreda: 'Like any ramp up, there's always risks that we cannot envision today, and that's why the wider range'; 'We feel the guidance is still good.' On 2027: 'we do not expect any closure of facilities. We do not expect any major new manufacturing capacity that will support our revenue in 2027', and as a lesson from this year, new facilities coming up 'we will probably hedge them more for next year'.

Refunds: CFO Ahmed Pasha said Fluence has 'some IEPA refund' — 'a little over $10 million' recognized year to date — among the puts and takes in the guidance, with more to be recognized over time in Q4 and later; CEO Julian Nebreda: part is recognized now and part goes into inventory, recognized as that inventory converts into revenue.
quarterly_data.figure: a little over $10 million recognized year to date

quarterly_data.signal: Metric definition (CEO Julian Nebreda): Fluence's deployed-megawatts metric counts only projects that have reached substantial completion, while revenue is recognized significantly earlier, when equipment is delivered to site and title transfers (CFO: percentage of completion) — so deployed megawatts lag revenue; 'We probably need to amend our definition to align it more with the revenue recognition definition.' Revenue recognition follows project milestones, the CEO said: 'in a period of 18 months, you recognize the full revenue'.

Data-center go-to-market (CEO Julian Nebreda): Fluence went to hyperscalers first 'because we know that's the door for the developers'; the hyperscalers have referred Fluence to developers that work for them. Developers 'are in a much of a hurry' compared with hyperscalers, and that market is 'a lot more active', moving from leads to pipeline to orders more quickly. Most activity and the contracts signed so far are in the U.S., but Fluence is also looking at other markets with some of the same hyperscalers and developers, where 'our global footprint will help us on capturing that demand more globally'. CEO on scale: 'our big issue is scaling this company', and 'scale drives competitiveness'.
